 Journals , PS: Political Science and Politics

 Forecasting the 2026 US Midterm Elections 
 When Do Prediction Markets Improve Election Forecasts? Evidence from Matched U.S. Races 
 By Jack Rossbach , Georgetown University in Qatar 
 When do prediction-market prices improve a statistical election forecast? I evaluate this question for a fixed panel of Senate and gubernatorial races in 2022 and 2024. Ninety days before Election Day, averaging a Bayesian polls-and-fundamentals model with prediction-market prices improves upon the model forecast, reducing its Brier score by 28 percent in both cycles. The reduction falls to 5 percent in 2022 and 14 percent in 2024 at 30 days, and by the day before the election, averaging raises error in 2022 and makes little difference in 2024. The pattern persists after removing the most influential races, under alternative poll-error assumptions, and in a separate comparison with archived forecasts for 56 presidential jurisdictions. The early-horizon improvement is larger in races with sparse polling and in competitive races. Selected 2024 and 2026 races illustrate how model-market disagreements evolve as later polls become available.
 Read the full article. 
 The editorial team at PS: Political Science & Politics is pleased to announce the release of articles that will make up a Special Issue on Forecasting the 2026 US Midterm Elections.  
 “Coupled with the unique circumstances of the 2026 election, it’s a tough one to call. Will we see a return to the fundamentals of American election forecasting, or will it prove a challenge to the widespread beliefs about American electoral behaviour?” – Dr Debra Lynn Leiter.
